title: The RTX 5090’s 16-pin connector just got a free pin-by-pin watchdog
summary: RTX Lens, a free open-source Windows app, reads per-pin current from Asus ROG Astral GPUs, WireView Pro II and MSI PSUs.
body: A developer known as Codeh4ck released a free, open-source Windows app , RTX Lens, to help assuage melting power connector fears for owners of powerful RTX 5080 and 5090 GPUs. The app can read per-pin current information on Asus Astral cards, the WireView Pro II GPU monitoring device from Thermal Grizzly, and MSI MPG Ai1300TS/Ai1600TS PSUs, enabling an optional shutdown for persistent warnings. It works by reading current at the GPU, PSU, or both ends of the cable, and can even notify you by phone to provide extra protection for your investment. The project’s README says that the app allows reading of “GPU power, pin currents, and temperatures at a glance.” The per-pin monitoring is the important part here, as the 12V-2x6 connection carries current on six 12V pins with a rating of about 9A, with Asus’s warning at 9.2A, and exceeding the per-pin limit has led to melted connectors . An RTX 5090 is rated at 575W of board power, which is close to the connector’s 600W rating. This led to the app’s construction, the developer says, due to “double paranoia about the 12VHPWR connector melting, since I own 2 5090s.” (Image credit: RTX Lens ) For supported Asus ROG Astral RTX 5080 and 5090 …

body: A wall of 100 Noctua PC fans was built by maker Sasa Karanovic because "why not." There's a little more to it, though, as the Toronto-based electronics and 3D printing expert wanted to test the capabilities of his new open-source open-hardware OpenFAN XL fan controller . A video shows the setup and control of a 10x10 Noctua fan grid controlled via the 10 headers on the controller. A 50x2 setup was also shown working off the controller. Karanovic indicates that 100 fans was "no sweat" for the new controller, but it would max out at around 200 spinners in its current iteration. The maker explains in the video that they had this demo idea a while back but recently acquired 100 fans through a combination of "a ton of luck and a good friend." As the new OpenFAN XL controller has 10 headers, the natural first step in controlling them all was to make a grid of 10 x 10 units. That's a lot of fans, but there's also 200 fan grills, 800 screws, and oodles of wiring, including tens of fan splitters.
